text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG

- Chancellor Helmut Kohl's top deputy Wolfgang Schaeuble and Michael Glos, leader of the Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) reject criticism made by President Roman Herzog of political logjam over urgently needed reforms.
- Two conservative state justice ministers criticise planned penal reform which would impose harsher punishment for crimes against the person and be more lenient for crimes against property.
- Suspected anti-nuclear activists set fire to an electricity transformer station in Hamburg.
- Cabinet agrees that anybody who buys a car battery without handing in the old one must pay a forfeit of 15 marks.
- Nobody is required to switch to the euro single currency until 2002, according to an interim report approved by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet.
HANDELSBLATT
- Dollar climbs to its highest level against the mark since February 1994 -- almost 1.74 marks -- despite commments by central bankers and finance ministers in Washington.
- German diversified industry group Viag AG shatters its unit trading and services group Kloeckner & Co AG, with plans to sell two of its five divisions and refocus its business.
- The Handelsblatt economic growth barometer for eastern Germany climbs to 5.6 percent in April, up 0.3 percent compared to March.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Ruling coaltion and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) look ready to debate reforms again after tax talks broke down last week.
- Buyers of new car batteries must hand in old ones, government decides.
- German OeTV and DAG unions found joint sister union for the employees of international public organisations in Germany such as the planned European central bank.
- Dollar climbs strongly, reaching 1.7325 marks.
DIE WELT
- Political parties greet President Herzog's appeal for reform. CDU's Schaeuble denies there is a policy logjam.
- Saxony premier Kurt Biedenkopf sticks by his criticism of Kohl's decision to run again for the chancellorship in next year's general elections.
- Inhabitants of Germany's big cities are dog lovers -- 95,461 dogs live in Berlin alone, 27 dogs for every 1,000 inhabitants.
